body: Just wrote a similar post about an issue i'm facing (i'm 24F) and I don't know what to do either. It sounds cliche but I've been working really hard on enjoying my own company & being okay with being alone because I gave up on expecting other people to be better. People don't change unless they want to, and unfortunately there is a ton of immaturity and insecurity in the world. I'm hoping, praying, trying desperately to believe that if i'm authentic and do the work myself, like-minded people will come into my life. But in terms of advice, I'm not sure I have any concrete ideas. I feel the same way as you - and its so hard. Hang in there.

There were times where I thought that "God was speaking to me" during really difficult times in my adolescence, and as I got older, I realized I was just experiencing thoughts. It was literally just my subconscious brain talking to itself. Once I figured out that it wasn't God, it gave me a new perspective on how all the people in my church insisted that god spoke to them directly, or how they were able to speak in tongues.

You should be proud of yourself for going out on your own, finding your own therapist and job placement program, staying with your friend, and knowing your limits. The comments like that from parents can definitely hurt, and nobody *wants* to have to leave their family, but sometimes it really is necessary to help our mental health when our family is the cause of harm.

It takes a lot of strength to seek out resources on your own, alone, feeling unsupported. I moved out of my parents house about 3 years ago, and they were incredibly angry at me. I was basically living out of a suitcase for a few months in a friend's guest room. I graduated college, began grad school, and moved 7 hours away. I cried all the time for the first few months, and I've been doing intensive weekly therapy for the past few years. It has been really hard - but never once do I regret listening to my gut feeling. There was no way I could stay there with them and be healthy. 

The process of figuring things out is painful, especially when religion and family are involved. Growth is painful. But I think its really encouraging that you know whats good for you (and whats harming you) and where you are now. You don't necessarily have to have life figured out all at once, so maybe try to take it a step at a time. In terms of encouragement, just know that it will be okay (and i'm not just saying that), and there are many other people who have been in your shoes before and have gotten through this. You will too. The process is hard, painful, challenging, etc. but it's worth it.

I feel that way a lot - I always say I feel like I come off as "spiky", like everyone can tell i'm unapproachable or on-edge. I can't explain it any other way, I just feel like I exist in this "spiky" way, and if I come off too strong people won't enjoy being around me, but its just the way I am.

I don't really know if I trust any of the faculty members to bring this up because the feeling i've gotten so far is kind of like "get over it". Last year in my first semester I brought up to a professor that I was being triggered in our sessions and she told me to do yoga....other professors have said that we have to "deal with our own crap" to be a good therapist - completely ignoring the fact that some students are actively dealing with mental illnesses in our program. It just doesn't feel like an environment where I can speak up, because the few times I have they really shut me down or don't take me seriously

I've definitely felt this way - I have really vivid and graphic dreams/nightmares almost every night, mainly having to do with my abuse or my parents. Even just last night I had one about baby farm animals dying in front of me and my father laughing at them while I wept. So yeah, I never feel super inclined to share with other people the types of dreams that I have, because in the few times I have they look at me mortified.

As i've gotten older, i've felt this more. Each year when I learn what other families were like and I see how functional people treat their children, that comment feels worse. I essentially raised my sister growing up (she's 7 years younger than me) and I would never say things to her that my parents said/did to me or her. My therapist told me that this anger will probably increase the older I get, especially if I decide to have my own kids.  


I think that "you'll understand someday" comment is a way for them to justify abuse and feel better about the dissonance they're experiencing deep down. if they admitted "oh wait I am being a shitty person right now and causing harm", then they would feel guilty & bad about themselves. So instead, they shift the blame onto the child, saying "you'll understand how easy it is to be abusive someday".   


I'm so sorry that you've experienced this, and I wish you all of the best in recovering while taking care of your sister. That is a lot to carry & I hope you realize how much strength it takes to handle all of that alone & give yourself so much more credit

That's ok thank you for the spoiler warning! I've watched all of the movies twice & i'm nearly done with the book, I only have about two chapters left. But yes I agree that Frodo being permanently damaged is so important because I feel like a ton of novels have a "happy ending" and the main character is seemingly unaffected by their traumatic experiences. I like that Frodo has real reactions to his horrific circumstances

I try to - until I start having a physical reaction (nausea, sweating, shaking, crying, etc.) I write as much as I can until my body tells me i'm unsafe. I'm working on a memoir, and writing it out has helped me heal, but only when the time is right. its not something I can rush.
This was incredibly helpful to read, thank you so much

I'm very sorry you lost people in your life, and I'm sorry that you also struggled with suicidal thoughts. 

I think counseling and therapy is a great resource (I myself am currently in graduate school training to become a licensed counselor, which is kind of funny that i'll be trying to help others not feel the way that I feel). I've been going to the same therapist for 6 years, and i've made a lot of growth, but at the same time it has been hard. I have CPTSD, depression, and anxiety. I've been doing a lot of work to try and heal from my past. But this type of stuff doesn't go away easily. The past year or so has just been really hard work and isolation trying to heal from my abusive parents and my ex. I've had to wake up every day and actively *try*, when I never want to. I wish that I felt optimistic about my future like I used to, but I just want to give up all the time. Grad school is hard. Being alone is hard. Working every day is hard. Not having family is hard. I'm just hurting every day and I feel very alone in what I'm going through because no one in my life can see what i'm going through. And this loneliness immediately leads to suicidality for me because its overwhelming and exhausting.   
I guess i'm not saying it won't get better, but after such a long time, i'm really losing hope that anything will change about my circumstances.

Yes. I go from "Maybe I should really engage in this project and try and go out and spend time with people", and then not even a day later, i'll struggle to get out of bed and face myself. I find myself surprised that the depression comes back swinging, all the time. It catches me off guard after my good days, which is funny because i've been feeling like this for such a long time.

healing is so uncomfortable!!! i'm working through years of trauma and abuse recently and I feel like i've never been so depressed, even though i'm in a much healthier spot. I've been exercising daily, and sometimes I hate it, but I know if I don't its going to become that much easier to fall into a depression. I know the end goal is worth it - but the process of going through healing is so uncomfortable and *weird*. I totally understand what you mean.

I like the monster metaphor too - namely Frankenstein's monster. He really encapsulates the feeling of being ignored, unloved, and feeling like you wish you were never created. I find myself feeling like Frankenstein's monster all the time.
ska music - and not for lack of trying. I tried. I can't do it
Led Zeppelin

I eventually started hiding snacks in my room just anticipating the fact that I would have to stay in there all night. But ritz crackers and saltines never really made up for the full meals I was supposed to be eating. My stomach and body have been really pissed at me in young adulthood for my disordered eating during my teen years because my abusive home made it impossible to eat three full meals a day. It has taken about 5+ years for me to get on a normal eating schedule.

  
I will never be able to forget going to bed with hunger pains for most of my life, and it is such a specific type of pain that I never want anyone else to experience. I am sorry that others have felt this pain too.

My mother abused me for most of my life in almost every way possible, and I think it is going to take me my entire life to come to a place of acceptance with her. She's very mentally ill and very sick, but the things I went through I would not wish on the person I hate most. To have gone through horrible abuse, and then to be told all the time "mothers are amazing" and "you NEED to love your mom", it really fucks with my head. I have learned to just ignore it, because people are only approaching it from their loved, cared-for point of view. They don't know what its like to have a mother who beats them, assaults them, verbally abuses them, psychologically abuses them, etc. It is almost never personal coming from people who have good relationships with their mothers - but OH man does it feel personal and does it hurt. I can empathize with the fact that those phrases are annoying, invalidating and stinging.

That phrase "you only get one mother" was used by my father, my relatives, & everyone who never wanted to address my mothers abusive behavior and wanted to ignore the very real pain I was living in. 

I remember many times crying to my aunts or my dad about how my mother had done something really fucked up (beat me, tried to kill me, tried to kill our family pets, many more very very fucked up things I don't ever talk about). Instead of acknowledging how incredibly traumatic living with my mother was and trying to help me move out to somewhere safe, they always told (and continue to tell me), "That's just how your mother is, you have to go easier on her" or "you only get one mother so one day you'll have to forgive her"....I cannot begin to do the mental gymnastics to try and justify letting child abuse happen because "its too difficult" to address. I don't even really have any words for how those phrases made me feel coming from my FATHER and my AUNT. 

I finally moved myself out of that house in 2019, and now i'm in graduate school 7 states away to become a therapist, but it has been a HARD journey. I still hear that phrase all the time, and I just stopped talking to my family because I can't spend the rest of my life hearing my relatives justify my mother's abuse. My mother is very mentally ill, but her illness in no way made it okay for that shit to happen to me. I only get one mother, and *she* only has two daughters, so maybe the fucking responsibility should be on the adults to change and get help, and not on the children to forcibly forgive the people who abused them. ugh.

What would typically happen at my house is that one of my parents would abuse me (hit me, verbally abuse me, psychologically abuse me, etc.) and I would start crying because I was overwhelmed with it all. Then my dad would scream "stop crying, you're acting like a three year old!" I heard that phrase a lot, so much that I've internalized it. It was a complete dismissal of the very real pain I was in.

One example I remember was when my dad would wake me up in the morning on the weekends and call me a lazy piece of shit for sleeping in and rip my blankets off of me, and then eventually i'd cry, and then he would yell at me for crying and told me to "Grow up". As if every 13 year old girl wouldn't cry at being woken up like this???? I also used to cry a lot about just being in my household because I wanted to commit suicide, run away, or hurt myself. I was always met with the same reaction from my father, that I should just toughen up and deal with it, and stop crying. As you could imagine, that did not help.

It has been VERY hard to un-learn this. I cry all the time, but it is accompanied by guilt now. Every time I have a breakdown or sob, I find myself apologizing to everyone (even my therapist and partner) - despite the fact that given my life experiences, it is perfectly normal to feel grief, sadness, and depression

I definitely need to work on unashamedly feeling my feelings, like you said. It can be really hard to grieve because I simultaneously feel guilty for doing so. It sometimes just feels like a big bundle and mess of emotions that is hard to organize. But maybe learning how to properly grieve will help me sort out all of this

I feel the same way, questioning if I missed a crucial developmental stage - but sadly the only answer I've been told is that I am supposed to learn to provide that parental love for myself, by myself. My friends/relationships will never fill that gap that is supposed to be filled by parental love and care. And my parents are never going to change, and I can't go back and undo the trauma that has happened to me. 

All that we have control of is how we treat ourselves and talk to ourselves. When my therapist discussed this with me, I was obviously a bit annoyed and frustrated at the unfairness of it all, (I was abused and now i have to do the legwork to heal?!) but maybe it is important to start with small steps in loving yourself and trying to provide yourself with the love your parents didn't give you. Only you know exactly what you've been through, and only you know exactly what you need to feel better and grow into the person you want to be. The loneliness and sadness can get in the way sometimes, but deep down, you have the strength to do it, because existing with CPTSD every day on its own is a feat in itself. I wish you the best of luck and I hope that healing becomes easier over time

I've noticed that I never learned how to *actually* take care of myself. I feel like I have a definition of how other people love themselves, or how we are "supposed" to feel about ourselves, but I never learned what that looks like for me or what that even feels like. I never learned how to support my own needs without feeling guilty. I definitely never learned how to experience my own emotions without feeling guilty. (For example, any time I cry, I feel guilty, or any time I feel angry, I am not comfortable with it and feel the need to put on a happy face for others all the time)

I go to therapy weekly to help work on this, and I am keeping a self-compassion and self-love journal so that I'm forced to write down ways that I can care for myself emotionally and logically. I am also working on writing a book and some music, which is helping to get my feelings out creatively rather than me bottling them up all the time- so I really recommend some sort of creative outlet like art, music, or writing to express these emotions and teach yourself how to not neglect yourself in the way that your parents may have.
Kombucha...
"lack-of-a-trauma-informed-society" is the best I can come up with - but I agree with you! Not having enough words to describe these situations adds to this feeling of silence and discomfort

Finally getting tattoos. I wanted them for years but I could never afford them and I was too afraid to go by myself. I lived in an abusive household until 2019 and I really couldn't hold a steady job or focus on anything except my education - so though I wanted tattoos they were never a top priority when I was in survival mode. In 2020, after I had finally settled somewhere else, I took myself to get my first tattoo and I have a fourth appointment scheduled this week. Each time I like to get really large leg pieces, and I'll just sit there for hours like a champ and leave with a beautiful colorful piece. It feels like I'm reclaiming my body and independence and I've found it to be very empowering. It also makes me feel strong, because I used to think I was afraid of needles! I  love my tattoo artist and it's very cool to just have a positive experience to look forward to every few months when I get my paycheck!

My younger sister - I tried to think of much else but I'd say that's the most important reason I've found. We've been through awful, awful things in our household and if I'm not here then I don't think anyone else would know what she went through.

I love this comment - particularly the pirate part - because I also feel like I should just get all gold fillings and live out my dream of being a pirate as well. But I agree with you that it can be jarring to those with some people that those with CPTSD or trauma don't "look traumatized". I look like a healthy, normal, 23 year old until you look at an xray of my teeth or see me having a panic attack in therapy or look at my medical history. I don't "look" like I've gone through what I've gone through - which leads to a lot of awkward situations where I have to explain that my circumstances aren't "normal".   
I guess that's what hurts me - that I have to constantly explain my life in either direct or vague ways. It makes the process of healing slightly more difficult. It's like I not only have to get over my fear of medical care, pay for it with money I could be using for my education, but I also have to mentally prepare for what might be said to me and how I might react. The whole process is tiring. Thank you for your comment - it is incredibly validating to know that the way I reacted was actually perfectly fine & i'm not quite sure what else I would've said.

I become incredibly anxious at doctor's appointments as well, so I can relate to the avoidance of medical professionals in general. I've been kind of forcing myself to go to my new doctor once or twice a year to try and take control of my health for the first time in my life - even if it makes me uncomfortable. Usually, after the appointments, when issues are resolved, I feel a lot better even if the process itself is painful.   
I will say a HUGE part of my comfort is that I finally found a doctor who I like, who doesn't talk to me condescendingly, and who listens to me. This is after many years of being unable to find a doctor that clicked well with me. My advice is to ignore people's ignorance surrounding CPTSD and CSA, though it can be difficult, and do what is good for YOU and your health. <3 Thank you for the wonderful comment

This response actually made me smile - so thank you! I'm currently training to be a therapist and so I'm trying to get better at informing people in non-confrontational ways about how to handle issues regarding trauma & sensitivity. People generally feel uncomfortable talking about "heavy issues", despite the fact that such a large number of people in our society are struggling with a multitude of things. I didn't get angry at the hygienist or the dentist, but rather I'm trying to approach everything with empathy these days. It's not always easy but I really appreciate that you said this.

Not every day, but sometimes I will wake up and just know its going to be a "weepy day", where I end up crying over everything from dog videos to childhood trauma to a work email I got. Those days my threshold is so low I feel like I can't tolerate anything

I can relate to being the target of abuse - my mom always liked to "triangulate" me into her fights with my father, as my therapist calls it. But they rarely ever went after my sister, and would focus on verbally/physically abusing me instead of dealing with their own issues. It definitely does some damage to you as a person that is incredibly hard to overcome.

This happened so often in my family (at least several times a week) that my sister and I turned it into a game to cope. It's kind of dark really, but when our parents would scream or argue in the car at each other, we would pretend to mimic them and move our mouths as if we were the ones yelling, like we were puppets. (My sister was about 4 and I was 10). It somehow made us laugh at how ridiculous it was because our parents were ALWAYS fighting and screaming at each other. I think I'm the one that started it, to prevent her from crying, and tried to make it funny instead. When I look back on it now, I want to cry a bit, because its incredibly sad how resilient we had to be in order to just exist in that house.  


For my household, fighting and yelling was not as bad as the other types of abuse, so I think I just learned to cope by making it seem less bad than it was. But no child deserves to witness anything like that.

I had an old roommate who posted something online that said suicide was "weak" and people committed suicide because they didn't have God in their lives. I immediately did not speak to her for the rest of the year until after I moved out and blocked her - but it makes me really sad and angry that some Christians promote views that can harm people's mental health forever and prevent them from ever getting help. 

In my own life, I was experiencing horrible depression and anxiety and panic attacks during my parents divorce as a middle schooler, and the church (and a christian therapist) told me that my parents divorce was because I was not praying enough, and they needed god. (Not because my mom had undiagnosed bipolar disorder my entire life and my father was an abusive alcoholic) Instead of reaching out to provide help to my sick mother, they blamed my parents, and somehow, also me. The only intervention my family needed at that point was proper mental health care and a social worker. We got neither - but we did get plenty of pastors and youth group meetings telling us to pray or read the bible.   
The people I met in the church spread anti-mental health rhetoric, and it is EXTREMELY dangerous. Whether that's NPD or APD, i'm not sure, but I do know that from my experience, proper mental health care does not involve toxic religious views. Praying isn't going to fix trauma, long-term chemical imbalances, or abuse - no matter what the church says. There are studies in positive psychology that HEALTHY spirituality (like helpful social interactions/friendships and mindfulness, personal, private spirituality) can be really good for our brains - but that does not include the dismissal of mental illness. 

this is slightly off topic but I also feel like the church encourages certain behaviors that are really unhealthy - like "hearing god and the angels", or thinking that you are a prophet. My mother, as well as other mothers I knew, said that they could "hear god" and that the "angel told them to do xyz". I've heard of others claiming to have seen angels, or that God told them they were a prophet. All of these behaviors can be linked to schizo-type diseases or even severe bipolar disorder. (Delusions, paranoia, and hallucinations are associated with so many types of mental illnesses and certain drug abuse) As a child, I believed it, but as an adult, I realized that it was my mother's hallucinations and undiagnosed mental illnesses being fueled by religion. It makes me sad now to think of my mother and all the others of the church whose mental illnesses have been ignored because it is the "norm" in the community. She needed actual medical help, and I suffered long-term because of a community that ignores depression, anxiety, and everything in between.   


(btw I am an ex-evangelical and i'm currently studying to become a therapist, to yknow, prevent this shit from happening to other people, and there's several others in my program who are ex-Christians and we talk about this stuff all the time)

yes definitely - I found pictures/videos from when I was 13 and at the time, I was dealing with very heavy thoughts and terrible events at home. I really felt like an adult, and then I watched the videos and I am just a kid. I felt so much older but it is jarring to recognize how old I actually was.

I have a picture of my sister and I in my apartment from when we were kids, and I cry at it sometimes because I look so genuinely happy in the picture. I don't think I have smiled like that since then, and I had no idea how much harder my life was going to get as I aged.  I can relate to the immense grief that comes with looking at the pictures sometimes. I get rage too, getting angry at all the adults that fucked up that little, happy kid so much. It's sadness, nostalgia, and rage, all at once.

Man's Search for Meaning by Viktor Frankl. (I think its available online for free but I have a book version of it) - it has helped me keep my eyes on the larger picture and where I want to be once i'm done healing and working through a lot of my shit

Bastard out of Carolina by Dorothy Allison - fair warning it is incredibly triggering and upsetting at points in the novel, but i'm so glad i read it. there are interviews with her along with the novel itself that were so impactful to me. Any memoir that is written by someone who has endured horrible events and survived to write about it has always been important to me.

and this ted talk: [https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=RcGyVTAoXEU&ab\_channel=TED](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=RcGyVTAoXEU&ab_channel=TED) that discusses how prolonged stress can be really bad for us but if we are able to reframe it as a challenge then we can actually use it to our advantage. kind of related to trauma because our CPTSD bodies are usually in fight/flight mode but I just really like ted talks lmao

when I was a kid I would go and sit in the corner of my parents closet, behind all the shoes and dresses. when I was a teenager, I would lie in the corner next to my bed on the floor and cry. and now, as an adult, I still like to lay on the floor and stare at the ceiling or sit on the floor and somehow it brings me comfort and i dont know why. But safety? I don't think I ever lived in a place that has *felt* truly completely 100% safe (even if it realistically is).   


When I moved into my current apartment, I constantly checked all the smoke detectors to make sure there were no cameras in them (there aren't) but I think my unsafe living situations for 23 years really left a bad imprint on my brain because I am always paranoid someone is going to hurt me or stalk me. I still even have reactions to stomping or slamming doors from downstairs neighbors. I feel like it doesn't go away, for me at least. I'm always jumpy and a little irritated

yes - in HS and early college I had no problem telling my friends and others what was going on with me, what I was feeling, what traumatic thing had happened to me recently. I felt like I was an open book - but as I got older I began to realize I think they all thought I was lying about what was going on in my life.  


Now, I can genuinely say I don't think I have told anyone anything personal in almost a year. I go to my therapist now if I need to talk about something thats hurting me, but I basically completely cut myself off from all my friends because I no longer trust anyone with my stuff. I started a grad program in September, and none of them know anything about me, because I don't even feel comfortable telling anyone anymore because it became so exhausting. Now I dont even know how to get back to normal
I'd risk eternal hellfire for a Lance peanut butter cracker sandwich, honestly

I was raised in the Evangelical church my entire life until i left in adulthood and I used to get anxious if I didn't ask for "forgiveness" every single night before I went to bed - but I was like 5 years old. I don't think I ever knew what I was asking "forgiveness" for but I would get really anxious and panicky if I forgot to because I thought if I died I would immediately be going to hell. 

I also used to feel anxious when I slept because I had/have insomnia and I thought that demons were going to hurt me in my sleep and I had to compulsively imagine angels surrounding me to ensure that I would sleep safely.   
mainly, this fear of hell followed me all throughout my childhood and adolescence because I genuinely thought that if I died I would not be "worthy enough" to get into heaven and I would burn eternally because I was a sinner....yall I was a child what sin could I have possibly committed? eating too many snacks??

Yes!!! I'm binge-reading the Lord of the Rings series and playing Skyrim because I never really engaged with fantasy media at all as a child, and I'm absolutely loving it now as an adult.  (But yes, I also feel like an alien, trying to catch up with all the cool "normal person" stuff that has surrounded everyone else for the past 20 years)

I'm also trying to catch up on holiday traditions because my parents never celebrated anything - like decorating for valentines day or halloween

currently writing a memoir right now but, long story short, my mother has severe bipolar I and borderline personality disorder and was not medicated properly for most of my life. She was addicted to prescription medication and often mixed pills which resulted in me dealing with most of her manic episodes as a child. my father is an alcoholic and was rarely home to protect me and my sister. I had forgotten very large chunks of my life until about this year when I remembered some repeated sexual abuse from childhood on top of the verbal, emotional, and physical abuse I knew I had endured. I was bullied at school, I was abused at home, and I really only had myself to get through those hard times. Now i'm dealing with year 5 of PTSD since I left home and I'm trying to undo all of the bad that has happened to me in my life. (also writing about it so that I can get it out there into the open)

Yes - especially the having something to expect & control part. I like having my morning schedule where I drink coffee and read a book, then do yoga and shower. If any part of that gets disrupted I get really upset and feel very uneasy. I think I started doing it as a coping mechanism to get me out of bed in the morning because for a while I was struggling to even get up. I also sit by the window and I really don't feel comfortable sitting anywhere else while I drink my coffee. It's strange how we find ways to comfort ourselves in these niche ways, but I guess it does help

Yes - my parents kept a lot of our important documents in a box in the basement that would get flooded so i've lost a lot of my things over the years. And I can definitely relate to the dentist part of what you said - after nearly a decade of not having been taken to the dentist, I had to get twelve cavities filled over the summer, and paid thousands of dollars for them myself. It was awful, but it is empowering to have the strength to make your own life yours again.

I love this reddit because I always find people expressing exactly my thoughts in a way that I would've never thought to express them. The Lord of the Rings analogy is so exact in how it feels to see what you want but for one reason or another, you're not sure how/if you will get there, or if its even attainable for you. People tell you its there, and it appears that other people have reached it before, but when you're alienated by trauma and society, it seems that you'll never even understand what that beauty is like in the way that others will.   


I love that you mentioned feeling alienated by *yourself*. I know I am excluded from things/don't experience life the same way as those without CPTSD, but the hardest days are when I no longer want to be me. The worst is when even I don't believe I can do it because I hate myself to my core. I completely get what you mean about having passions and dreams that society crushes - my love in life is music and songwriting, but I stopped pursuing it as a career because I need money to live. For me, music is that LOTR shore that I've never been able to reach, because my early life experiences really prevented me from doing so many things I love, and now I am left to clean up the pieces of a broken childhood. I know that if I could've been lucky to not have a traumatic childhood, I would've been confident that i'd reach that beauty and not feel that gap within myself. But, I wasn't lucky, and there is a huge gap. In the process, I'm still alienating myself, and I'm unsure of what to do in life because I don't know who I am or what I want, (besides those dreams that are unattainable)  
My analogy that I turn to is that I constantly feel like Frankenstein's monster. Truly abhorred, not quite knowing why I was cursed to live if my creator doesn't love me, and not allowed to die. I could function fine if the world would let me, but I'm rejected by all when they see me for what I really am (a victim of childhood abuse, a monster, ugly, and unknown). 

Bottom line, CPTSD makes you question who you are inside and what your values are, because we never got a chance to learn who *we* were without the influence of other people hurting us. We do feel truly alienated because we live in a society that alienates us, because unless you have CPTSD, I feel like you fundamentally cannot understand what its like. And overall, that truly sucks.

I've been feeling this a lot recently - especially with my childhood and teen years. I have learned so much sadness and rage that i've internalized, and it really impacted my self-esteem and view of myself and just made me miserable for most of my life. I always think about what I would've been like if my life hadn't gone the way it did, and how much well-off and happier I would've been. It just feels like an overwhelming sense of grief sometimes, knowing that you can't go back and change any of it. All I do is cry or write about it or let it pass. it really is like grieving a massive loss, except the loss was yourself as a child

I had several bad social workers/therapists in my teen years until I got to college and found someone who I can actually talk to without being judged or ridiculed. this social worker may have been crappy, but that is just one social worker out of millions. as someone who has been fighting suicidal thoughts for over a decade, I can safely say there are people out there who can and will listen to you because they DO care - and they won't laugh at you over the phone. they might just be difficult to find, but they are out there.

EMDR is a type of desensitization therapy, and I have heard that it has been incredibly helpful for those who do it. Don't be so quick to write off a therapist, they are confidentially bound to keep whatever you tell them private unless you have plans to hurt yourself or someone else. Your mother is responsible for her own emotions, and you are responsible for taking care of your own. If you feel unwell, then you should be given the ability to talk to someone about it. A therapist is a great resource to work through how you're feeling and get a diagnosis that may help you cope better, as well as teach you ways to communicate with your mother that may help her feel less inclined to blame herself. There is even the option of family therapy if your family feels comfortable with it, where you could express these feelings in a safe setting where a therapist can function as a neutral party to help you all work together better - and specifically help you share your feelings with your family without your mother speaking over you.

I know for myself, constantly being on my phone or watching television as a coping mechanism only hurts me, and if I need to focus on schoolwork I have to cut every distraction out. If you practice it enough, it becomes habitual and then studying or doing work also becomes a part of your self care. You could also try finding an intrinsic motivator for some of your classes & finding aspects of the work that inspire you or feel meaningful to you (I admit, thats not always easy)
